content.prompt: The ratio of length to width of a rectangle is $3:2$. Find the rectangle’s dimensions if its perimeter is $120\text{ cm}$.

answer.worked:
Let the length and width be $3x\text{ cm}$ and $2x\text{ cm}$, respectively.

$$\begin{align*}2(3x)+2(2x)&=120\\10x&=120\\x&=12\end{align*}$$

The length is $3\times12=36\text{ cm}$ and the width is $2\times12=24\text{ cm}$.

content.prompt: The width of a rectangle is $4\text{ cm}$ longer than its length. Find the rectangle’s dimensions if its perimeter is $36\text{ cm}$.

answer.worked:
Let the length and width be $x\text{ cm}$ and $(x+4)\text{ cm}$, respectively.

$$\begin{align*}2x+2(x+4)&=36\\4x+8&=36\\4x&=28\\x&=7\end{align*}$$

The length is $7\text{ cm}$ and the width is $7+4=11\text{ cm}$.

content.prompt: Find the minimum perimeter of a rectangle formed using $40$ square tiles of side $1\text{ cm}$.

answer.short:
$26\text{ cm}$.

The $5\text{ cm}\times8\text{ cm}$ arrangement has the smallest perimeter.
answer.worked:
The possible dimension pairs in centimetres are $(1,40)$, $(2,20)$, $(4,10)$ and $(5,8)$.

$$\begin{align*}P_{1,40}&=2(1)+2(40)=82\text{ cm}\\P_{2,20}&=2(2)+2(20)=44\text{ cm}\\P_{4,10}&=2(4)+2(10)=28\text{ cm}\\P_{5,8}&=2(5)+2(8)=26\text{ cm}\end{align*}$$

The minimum perimeter is $26\text{ cm}$.

teachingContext.methodNote: Use the taught rectangle perimeter formula to compare the whole-number factor pairs of 40.
teachingContext.mappingNote: Whole square tiles constrain the rectangle dimensions to integer factor pairs; no continuous optimisation is needed.

content.prompt: Luna measures three sides of a rectangle, and their lengths total to $27\text{ cm}$. Mateo measures three sides of the same rectangle, and their lengths total to $33\text{ cm}$. Find the perimeter of the rectangle.

answer.short:
$40\text{ cm}$.

Adding the two three-side totals gives three times the sum of adjacent sides.
answer.worked:
Let the adjacent side lengths be $a\text{ cm}$ and $b\text{ cm}$. The distinct three-side totals give $2a+b=27$ and $a+2b=33$.

$$\begin{align*}3a+3b&=27+33\\3(a+b)&=60\\a+b&=20\\P&=2(a+b)\\P&=40\text{ cm}\end{align*}$$

teachingContext.methodNote: Use equal opposite sides and the taught rectangle perimeter formula; combine the two side-sum equations.
teachingContext.mappingNote: The different totals must correspond to the two possible three-side sums. Their addition determines the perimeter without finding individual dimensions.

content.prompt: A rectangle of dimensions $x\text{ cm}\times y\text{ cm}$ has a perimeter of $10\text{ cm}$. If $x$ is increased by $50\%$ and $y$ is decreased by $50\%$, then the resulting rectangle has a perimeter of $6\text{ cm}$. Find $x$ and $y$.

answer.short:
$x=0.5,\quad y=4.5$; the original dimensions are $0.5\text{ cm}\times4.5\text{ cm}$.

Use the perimeter equations before and after the percentage changes.
answer.worked:
The original perimeter gives

$$\begin{align*}2x+2y&=10\\x+y&=5\end{align*}$$

The new dimensions are $1.5x\text{ cm}$ and $0.5y\text{ cm}$, so

$$\begin{align*}2(1.5x)+2(0.5y)&=6\\3x+y&=6\end{align*}$$

Subtract $x+y=5$ from $3x+y=6$:

$$\begin{align*}2x&=1\\x&=0.5\end{align*}$$

Substitute into $x+y=5$:

$$\begin{align*}0.5+y&=5\\y&=4.5\end{align*}$$

The original dimensions are $0.5\text{ cm}\times4.5\text{ cm}$.

teachingContext.methodNote: Use the rectangle perimeter formula and Example 1's algebraic modelling approach for both rectangles, then eliminate y.
teachingContext.mappingNote: Finding unknown dimensions from perimeter is the closest supplied catalogue skill; percentage changes create two simultaneous relationships.

answerEvidence.matchEvidence: Section A item 9 visibly gives x = 0.5 cm, y = 4.5 cm. The student dimensions are x cm and y cm; independently derived numerical values x = 0.5 and y = 4.5 give original perimeter 10 cm and changed perimeter 6 cm. The authored answer distinguishes these numerical variables from the physical dimensions.

content.prompt: Find the perimeter of each of the figures shown below. You may assume that anything that looks like a right-angle is a right-angle.

spec.description: Three-level orthogonal staircase with only its overall height and base labelled.
spec.mathematics: Overall height 12 m and width 20 m; intermediate step lengths are unspecified.
spec.answerVisibility: No derived lengths or answer shown.

answer.worked:
The horizontal boundary segments total $2\times20$ m, and the vertical boundary segments total $2\times12$ m.
$$\begin{align*}P&=2\times20+2\times12\\P&=64\,\mathrm{m}.\end{align*}$$

spec.description: Two rectangular notches; matching single ticks on five top horizontal segments and four notch vertical segments.
spec.mathematics: Base 30 m, outer height 18 m; all nine ticked segments have equal length.
spec.answerVisibility: Common segment length is not supplied.

answer.worked:
The five equal horizontal segments total $30$ m, so each ticked segment is $30\div5=6$ m. The four notch sides also have length $6$ m.
$$\begin{align*}P&=2\times30+2\times18+4\times6\\P&=120\,\mathrm{m}.\end{align*}$$

spec.description: Right trapezium with an unlabelled sloping right side.
spec.mathematics: Height 6 cm, top 4 cm, base 10 cm.
spec.answerVisibility: No auxiliary triangle or calculated side shown.

answer.worked:
The sloping side has horizontal difference $10-4=6$ cm and vertical difference $6$ cm. By Pythagoras,
$$\begin{align*}s&=\sqrt{6^2+6^2}\\s&=6\sqrt2\,\mathrm{cm}.\\P&=6+4+10+6\sqrt2\\P&=(20+6\sqrt2)\,\mathrm{cm}.\end{align*}$$

spec.description: Five-sided outline with a diagonal at the upper left.
spec.mathematics: Left height 9 m, right height 6 m, base 16 m, upper horizontal side 12 m.
spec.answerVisibility: Diagonal remains unlabelled.

answer.worked:
The diagonal has horizontal difference $16-12=4$ m and vertical difference $9-6=3$ m.
$$\begin{align*}s&=\sqrt{4^2+3^2}\\s&=5\,\mathrm{m}.\\P&=9+16+6+12+5\\P&=48\,\mathrm{m}.\end{align*}$$

spec.description: U-shaped orthogonal outline; arm widths and inner horizontal length are unspecified.
spec.mathematics: Outer heights 8 cm and 5 cm, left inner descent 6 cm, base 29 cm.
spec.answerVisibility: No derived dimensions shown.

answer.worked:
The inner horizontal edge is $8-6=2$ cm above the base, so the right inner side is $5-2=3$ cm. All horizontal boundary segments total $2\times29$ cm.
$$\begin{align*}P&=2\times29+8+6+3+5\\P&=80\,\mathrm{cm}.\end{align*}$$

spec.description: Trapezium with a dashed diagonal from upper-left to lower-right.
spec.mathematics: Base 14 cm, right height 8 cm, dashed diagonal 10 cm; top and left slope unknown.
spec.answerVisibility: Both unknown boundary lengths are omitted.

answer.worked:
Using the right-hand triangle, the top length is
$$\begin{align*}t&=\sqrt{10^2-8^2}\\t&=6\,\mathrm{cm}.\end{align*}$$
The left sloping side has horizontal difference $14-6=8$ cm and vertical difference $8$ cm.
$$\begin{align*}s&=\sqrt{8^2+8^2}\\s&=8\sqrt2\,\mathrm{cm}.\\P&=14+8+6+8\sqrt2\\P&=(28+8\sqrt2)\,\mathrm{cm}.\end{align*}$$

content.prompt: Three square tiles have sides of length $1$ cm, $2$ cm and $3$ cm. These three squares are arranged without overlap to create a figure of minimum possible perimeter. Find the perimeter of this figure.

answer.short:
$16\,\mathrm{cm}$

Place the $2$ cm and $1$ cm squares along one side of the $3$ cm square, with the smaller squares touching.
answer.worked:
Place the $2$ cm and $1$ cm squares side by side along a side of the $3$ cm square. Their shared edges with the large square total $3$ cm, and their mutual shared edge is $1$ cm.
$$\begin{align*}P&=4(1+2+3)-2(3+1)\\P&=16\,\mathrm{cm}.\end{align*}$$
This is minimal: the $2$ cm square can share at most $2$ cm with the large square, and the $1$ cm square can share at most $1$ cm with each of the other two squares. Thus the total shared length cannot exceed $4$ cm.

spec.description: Authored solution arrangement showing three non-overlapping adjoining squares.
spec.mathematics: Square sides 3, 2 and 1 cm; total shared edge length 4 cm.
spec.answerVisibility: Solution only.

teachingContext.methodNote: Square perimeter and addition of exposed boundary lengths.
teachingContext.mappingNote: The minimisation extends the taught boundary method by subtracting shared edges twice.

answerEvidence.matchEvidence: The Chapter 12 Section A answer list prints 11. 16 cm immediately after question 10. Independent arrangement of the 1 cm, 2 cm and 3 cm square tiles gives total shared length 4 cm and perimeter 16 cm.

content.prompt: Rectangle $A$ has dimensions $x\,\mathrm{cm}\times y\,\mathrm{cm}$. The rectangle may be cut in half vertically and its parts rearranged to give rectangle $B$, which has a perimeter of $30$ cm. Rectangle $A$ may also be cut in half horizontally and its parts rearranged to give rectangle $C$, which has a perimeter of $45$ cm. Find the perimeter of rectangle $A$.

spec.sourceRegion: Top of right column, continuation of question 12
spec.description: A, B and C appear in one paired comparison row. B has a solid horizontal join; C has a dashed vertical join. Decorative source red fill is omitted.
spec.mathematics: A has dimensions x by y; B comprises two x/2 by y pieces stacked; C comprises two x by y/2 pieces side by side.
spec.answerVisibility: Only A carries the supplied dimension labels.

answer.short:
$30\,\mathrm{cm}$

Add the two rearranged perimeter equations to obtain $x+y=15$ cm.
answer.worked:
Rectangle $B$ has dimensions $\frac{x}{2}$ cm by $2y$ cm; rectangle $C$ has dimensions $2x$ cm by $\frac{y}{2}$ cm.
$$\begin{align*}2\left(\frac{x}{2}+2y\right)&=30\\x+4y&=30\\2\left(2x+\frac{y}{2}\right)&=45\\4x+y&=45.\end{align*}$$
Adding the two simplified equations gives
$$\begin{align*}5x+5y&=75\\x+y&=15\\P_A&=2(x+y)\\P_A&=30\,\mathrm{cm}.\end{align*}$$

teachingContext.methodNote: Page 1 states P=2x+2y and demonstrates substituting algebraic dimensions into a perimeter equation.
teachingContext.mappingNote: The two cuts determine the dimensions of B and C; their perimeter equations determine the original perimeter.

answerEvidence.matchEvidence: The Chapter 12 Section A answer list prints 12. 30 cm. The source A/B/C diagrams and the stated 30 cm and 45 cm rearranged perimeters independently give x+4y=30 and 4x+y=45, hence the original perimeter is 30 cm.

content.prompt: The rectangular sheet depicted below has dimensions $20\text{ cm}$ by $30\text{ cm}$. It is folded to form the seven-sided vertically symmetric figure on the right. Find the perimeter of the seven-sided figure if quadrilateral $ABCD$ is a rectangle.

spec.sourceRegion: Question 14 paired sheet and folded figure
spec.description: Original landscape rectangle on the left; symmetric seven-sided folded outline on the right. The left strip is rectangle ABCD, with internal boundaries DC and CG. Decorative blue fills are omitted.
spec.mathematics: The sheet is 30 by 20. AB=CD=20 and AD=BC=5. The two central sloping sides meet at a right angle, giving the horizontal base length 20√2.
spec.answerVisibility: No numerical solution labels are printed in the question figure.

answer.short:
$(60+20\sqrt{2})\text{ cm}$.

The folded strips have widths $5\text{ cm}$; use Pythagoras for the base.
answer.worked:
$AB=CD=20\text{ cm}$. Since the two folded strips have equal widths,
$$\begin{align*}AD&=\frac{30-CD}{2}\\AD&=\frac{30-20}{2}\\AD&=5\text{ cm}.\end{align*}$$
The central triangle is right-angled, with its two sloping sides each $20\text{ cm}$. Let its base be $b$.
$$\begin{align*}b^2&=20^2+20^2\\b^2&=800\\b&=20\sqrt{2}\text{ cm}.\end{align*}$$
The outside boundary contains two sides of length $20\text{ cm}$, four sides of length $5\text{ cm}$ and the base.
$$\begin{align*}P&=2(20)+4(5)+20\sqrt{2}\\P&=(60+20\sqrt{2})\text{ cm}.\end{align*}$$

content.prompt: A right-angled triangle has a perimeter of $56$. Find its side lengths if each of these is an integer.

answer.worked:
Let the shorter sides be positive integers $a\le b$ and the hypotenuse be $c$. Then $c=56-a-b$.
$$\begin{align*}a^2+b^2&=(56-a-b)^2\\0&=3136-112a-112b+2ab\\ab-56a-56b&=-1568\\(56-a)(56-b)&=1568.\end{align*}$$
Since $a+b>c$ and $c>b\ge a$, we have $19\le c\le27$ and $1\le a\le18$. Thus $38\le56-a\le55$. The only divisor of $1568=2^5\times7^2$ in this interval is $49$.
$$\begin{align*}56-a&=49\\a&=7\\56-b&=1568\div49\\56-b&=32\\b&=24\\c&=56-7-24\\c&=25.\end{align*}$$
Check: $7+24+25=56$ and $7^2+24^2=49+576=625=25^2$. The side lengths are $7$, $24$ and $25$.

teachingContext.methodNote: Use perimeter as the sum of boundary lengths together with the right-triangle condition. The supplied teaching page does not demonstrate an integer-triple search or factorisation method.
teachingContext.mappingNote: The assessed task is finding an integer Pythagorean triple with a specified perimeter.

classification.difficultyReason: Trace equal-length relationships through a dissection and find the smallest consistent integer scale.

inlines.text: A rhombus is a quadrilateral all of whose sides are equal in length.

The figure below shows a large rhombus that has been dissected into equilateral triangles and rhombuses whose side lengths are all unequal positive integers. Find the smallest possible perimeter of the large rhombus.

spec.description: Complete planar rhombus dissection, with all original vertices, internal segment junctions, rhombuses and equilateral triangles; no numerical labels or decorative fills.
spec.mathematics: All edges use the same three triangular-lattice directions. Source topology retained, including the smallest central rhombus and adjoining smallest equilateral triangle.

answer.short:
$176$.

Use equal-side relationships to obtain $5x=2y$; the smallest integer scale has $x=2$ and $y=5$.
answer.worked:
Let $x$ be the side length of the smallest rhombus and $y$ the side length of the smallest equilateral triangle. Tracing equal sides and subtracting adjoining segments around the dissection gives two expressions for the side length of the leftmost rhombus:
$$\begin{align*}-8x+8y&=7x+2y\\6y&=15x\\2y&=5x.\end{align*}$$
Since $x$ and $y$ are positive integers, write $x=2k$ and $y=5k$, where $k$ is a positive integer. The smallest scale is $k=1$, giving $x=2$ and $y=5$.
The leftmost rhombus has side length $-8(2)+8(5)=24$. The adjoining upper-left triangle has side length $20$, so a side of the large rhombus is $24+20=44$.
$$\begin{align*}P&=4(44)\\P&=176.\end{align*}$$

teachingContext.methodNote: Use equal sides of each rhombus and equilateral triangle, segment addition and subtraction, then perimeter as four times the outer side. Teacher page 58 supplies the two consistency expressions.
teachingContext.mappingNote: The closest catalogue skill is length and perimeter problem solving; the principal demand is tracing segment relationships and selecting the smallest integer scale.

content.prompt: The wheel of a bicycle is $70$ cm in diameter.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Suppose the wheel makes $2$ revolutions per second. Calculate the speed of the cyclist in kilometres per hour, accurate to $2$ decimal places.

answer.worked:
$70\text{ cm}=0.7\text{ m}$. The distance travelled per revolution is
$$\begin{align*}C&=\pi d\\C&=0.7\pi\text{ m}.\end{align*}$$
At $2$ revolutions per second,
$$\begin{align*}v&=2\times0.7\pi\times\frac{3600}{1000}\\v&=5.04\pi\text{ km/h}\\v&\approx15.83\text{ km/h}.\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: If the cyclist is travelling at a speed of $40$ kilometres per hour, then how many revolutions per second does the wheel make, accurate to $2$ decimal places?

answer.worked:
The wheel travels $0.7\pi$ m per revolution. Convert the speed:
$$\begin{align*}v&=40\times\frac{1000}{3600}\\v&=\frac{100}{9}\text{ m/s}.\end{align*}$$
The number $n$ of revolutions per second is
$$\begin{align*}n&=\frac{100/9}{0.7\pi}\\n&=\frac{1000}{63\pi}\\n&\approx5.05\text{ rev/s}.\end{align*}$$

content.prompt: Consider the globe of the earth with a rope wrapped tightly around the equator. Now lengthen the rope by exactly $1$ metre. Finally, lift this (now loose) rope a uniform distance above the globe. Will a mouse fit under the rope?

inlines.text: Yes. The clearance is
Subtract the original circumference from the new circumference to find the increase in radius.

answer.worked:
Let $r$ m be Earth's radius, $R$ m the new rope radius and $C$ m the original rope length.
$$\begin{align*}C&=2\pi r\\C+1&=2\pi R.\end{align*}$$
Subtracting the first equation from the second gives
$$\begin{align*}1&=2\pi(R-r)\\R-r&=\frac{1}{2\pi}\text{ m}\\R-r&\approx0.159\text{ m}\\R-r&\approx15.9\text{ cm}.\end{align*}$$
Yes, a mouse can fit beneath a rope lifted about $15.9$ cm above the globe.

teachingContext.mappingNote: The unknown is an increase in radius determined from an increase in circumference, so the closest skill is finding a radius from circumference.

spec.description: An upright square overlaps a circle. Both top vertices lie on the circle; the bottom square edge is tangent at the circle's lowest point. The circle extends above the square and outside its vertical sides. Decorative blue fills are omitted.

answer.worked:
Let the square's side be $x$ and the circle's radius be $r$. Join the centre to the top-left vertex and the midpoint of the square's top side. The right triangle has side lengths $r$, $x/2$ and $x-r$.
$$\begin{align*}r^2&=\left(\frac{x}{2}\right)^2+(x-r)^2\\r^2&=\frac{x^2}{4}+x^2-2xr+r^2\\2xr&=\frac{5x^2}{4}\\r&=\frac{5x}{8}\\x&=\frac{8r}{5}.\end{align*}$$
The square's perimeter is
$$\begin{align*}P_{\text{square}}&=4x\\P_{\text{square}}&=\frac{32r}{5}\\P_{\text{square}}&=6.4r.\end{align*}$$
The circle's perimeter is $2\pi r$. Since $2\pi<6.4$, the square has the larger perimeter.

answer.worked:
The overlap is a $6\text{ cm}\times6\text{ cm}$ square. Each of the eight longer boundary segments has length $(30-6)/2=12\text{ cm}.$
$$\begin{align*}P&=8\times12+4\times6\\P&=120\text{ cm}\\A&=2(30\times6)-6^2\\A&=324\text{ cm}^2\end{align*}$$

children.prompt: Given the area of the cross is $28\text{ cm}^2$ and its perimeter is $32\text{ cm}$, find the dimensions of the rectangles.

inlines.text: The perimeter gives the length; subtract the square overlap when finding the area.

answer.worked:
Let the rectangle length be $L$ cm and its width be $w$ cm, with $0<w<L$. The exterior has eight segments of length $(L-w)/2$ and four of length $w$.
$$\begin{align*}P&=8\left(\frac{L-w}{2}\right)+4w\\P&=4L\\L&=\frac{32}{4}\\L&=8\end{align*}$$
Subtract the square overlap:
$$\begin{align*}A&=2Lw-w^2\\28&=16w-w^2\\28&=w(16-w)\end{align*}$$
The width is an integer between 1 and 7. Checking these values, only $w=2$ gives $w(16-w)=2\times14=28$. The rectangles are $2\text{ cm}\times8\text{ cm}$.

content.prompt: A square and an equilateral triangle each have a perimeter of $36$. Find the ratio of the area of the square to the area of the triangle.

answer.short:
$9:4\sqrt{3}$.

Find the triangle's altitude using Pythagoras, then compare the two areas.
answer.worked:
The square has side length $36\div4=9$, and the equilateral triangle has side length $36\div3=12$.

The triangle's altitude bisects its base. Let the altitude be $h$.

$$\begin{align*}h^2&=12^2-6^2\\h^2&=108\\h&=6\sqrt{3}\\A_{\text{square}}&=9^2\\A_{\text{square}}&=81\\A_{\text{triangle}}&=\frac{12\times6\sqrt{3}}{2}\\A_{\text{triangle}}&=36\sqrt{3}\end{align*}$$

Therefore the ratio is $81:36\sqrt{3}=9:4\sqrt{3}$.

spec.description: Outer regular hexagon with horizontal top and bottom sides; the shaded inner hexagon joins consecutive side midpoints and has vertical left and right sides. The six corner triangles remain unshaded.

answer.short:
$\dfrac34$.

Partition each hexagon into six equilateral triangles and compare their areas.
answer.worked:
Let the smaller and larger hexagons have side lengths $x$ and $y$. Each splits into six equilateral triangles, so
$$\begin{align*}A_{\text{small}}&=6\left(\frac{\sqrt3x^2}{4}\right)\\A_{\text{small}}&=\frac{3\sqrt3x^2}{2},\\A_{\text{large}}&=6\left(\frac{\sqrt3y^2}{4}\right)\\A_{\text{large}}&=\frac{3\sqrt3y^2}{2}.\end{align*}$$
A side of the smaller hexagon equals the perpendicular height of one of the larger hexagon's equilateral triangles. Hence
$$\begin{align*}x^2&=y^2-\left(\frac y2\right)^2\\x^2&=\frac{3y^2}{4}\\\frac{A_{\text{small}}}{A_{\text{large}}}&=\frac{x^2}{y^2}\\\frac{A_{\text{small}}}{A_{\text{large}}}&=\frac34.\end{align*}$$

content.prompt: A rectangle is dissected into four smaller rectangles by two straight cuts. Three of these have areas $3\text{ m}^2$, $4\text{ m}^2$ and $5\text{ m}^2$. Find the largest possible area of the fourth rectangle.

answer.short:
$\dfrac{20}{3}\text{ m}^2$.

The products of diagonally opposite areas are equal; place the missing area opposite $3\text{ m}^2$ to maximise it.
answer.worked:
The cuts form two rows and two columns. Let their heights be $h_1,h_2$ and widths be $w_1,w_2$. The products of diagonally opposite areas are equal because
$$\begin{align*}(w_1h_1)(w_2h_2)&=w_1w_2h_1h_2\\(w_1h_1)(w_2h_2)&=(w_2h_1)(w_1h_2).\end{align*}$$
The missing area can therefore be
$$\frac{3\times4}{5}=\frac{12}{5},\qquad \frac{3\times5}{4}=\frac{15}{4},\qquad \frac{4\times5}{3}=\frac{20}{3}.$$
Since $\dfrac{12}{5}<\dfrac{15}{4}<\dfrac{20}{3}$, the largest possible area is $\dfrac{20}{3}\text{ m}^2$.

content.prompt: A rectangle is dissected into four triangles by three straight cuts. The areas of three of these triangles are shown on the figure below. Find the area of the fourth triangle.

spec.description: Rectangle partitioned into four triangles, with the three given area labels retained inside their respective unshaded regions.
spec.mathematics: Cuts join the top-left corner to a bottom-edge point and a right-edge point, and join those two points. Given triangle areas are 3, 4 and 1. No dimensions or units are printed.
spec.answerVisibility: Only source givens are visible.

answer.short:
4 square units.

Express the three given triangle areas using the rectangle's dimensions to find its total area, then subtract $3+4+1$.
answer.worked:
Let the rectangle have height $x$, width $y$ and area $T=xy$. The bottom-left triangle has base $6/x$, and the top-right triangle has height $8/y$.

The bottom-right triangle therefore gives
$$\begin{align*}
\frac12\left(y-\frac6x\right)\left(x-\frac8y\right)&=1\\
xy-14+\frac{48}{xy}&=2\\
T+\frac{48}{T}-16&=0\\
T^2-16T+48&=0\\
(T-12)(T-4)&=0.
\end{align*}$$
The rectangle's area exceeds $3+4+1=8$, so $T=12$.
$$\begin{align*}
A_{\text{fourth triangle}}&=12-3-4-1\\
A_{\text{fourth triangle}}&=4.
\end{align*}$$
The fourth triangle has area 4 square units.

The diagonal divides the rhombus into two congruent triangles with sides $30$, $30$ and $48$ metres.

answer.short:

The shared diagonal is $41\text{ m}$. Add the right triangle’s area to the area found using Heron’s formula.

Draw the diagonal from the upper-left vertex to the bottom-right vertex. The right triangle has perpendicular sides $9\text{ m}$ and $40\text{ m}$.

$$\begin{align*}s&=\frac{15+28+41}{2}=42\\A_2&=\sqrt{42(42-15)(42-28)(42-41)}\\A_2&=\sqrt{42\times27\times14\times1}\\A_2&=126\text{ m}^2\\A_{\text{quadrilateral}}&=180+126\\A_{\text{quadrilateral}}&=306\text{ m}^2\end{align*}$$

content.prompt: The side lengths of a triangle are in the ratio $5:6:7$. The area of the triangle is $24\sqrt{6}\text{ cm}^2$. Find the side lengths of the triangle.

answer.short:
$10\text{ cm}$, $12\text{ cm}$ and $14\text{ cm}$.

Set the sides to $5k$, $6k$ and $7k$ and use Heron’s formula to obtain $k=2$.
answer.worked:
Let the side lengths be $5k$, $6k$ and $7k\text{ cm}$, where $k>0$.

$$\begin{align*}s&=\frac{5k+6k+7k}{2}\\s&=9k\\A&=\sqrt{9k(9k-5k)(9k-6k)(9k-7k)}\\A&=\sqrt{9k\times4k\times3k\times2k}\\A&=\sqrt{216k^4}\\A&=6\sqrt{6}\,k^2\end{align*}$$

Using the given area,

$$\begin{align*}6\sqrt{6}\,k^2&=24\sqrt{6}\\k^2&=4\\k&=2\end{align*}$$

The side lengths are $5(2)=10\text{ cm}$, $6(2)=12\text{ cm}$ and $7(2)=14\text{ cm}$.

content.prompt: Approximate the area of this quarter circle by finding the sum of the areas of the four regions depicted below. Hence, show that $\pi>3$.

spec.description: Radius-two quarter circle containing a unit square, two congruent trapezia and a triangle. Internal lines terminate at the arc-intersection vertices. Alternating light orange and unfilled regions identify the four components; curved gaps remain visible.
spec.mathematics: Centre (0,0), radius 2; internal partitions x=1 and y=1. Inscribed boundary vertices are (0,2), (1,sqrt(3)), (sqrt(3),1), (2,0). Only the four source labels 1 are printed.
spec.answerVisibility: No derived lengths, component areas or numerical approximation are printed.

answer.short:
$3$ square units; $\pi>3$.

The four inscribed regions have total area $3$, strictly less than the quarter-circle area $\pi$.
answer.worked:
The radius is $2$. At the point on the arc above the unit square, let the height above the base be $h$.

$$\begin{align*} h^2&=2^2-1^2\\ h^2&=3\\ h&=\sqrt3. \end{align*}$$
The square has area $1$. Each trapezium has parallel sides $1$ and $\sqrt3-1$ and perpendicular height $1$. The remaining triangle has perpendicular sides $\sqrt3-1$.

$$\begin{align*} A_{\text{inscribed}}&=1+2\left(\frac{1+(\sqrt3-1)}{2}\right)+\frac{(\sqrt3-1)^2}{2}\\ A_{\text{inscribed}}&=1+\sqrt3+2-\sqrt3\\ A_{\text{inscribed}}&=3. \end{align*}$$
The quarter circle has area $\frac14\pi(2)^2=\pi$. It also contains the curved gaps outside the straight inscribed boundary, so its area is strictly greater than $3$. Therefore, $\pi>3$.

Below is the graph of a parabola with equation $y=\frac14x^2$, plotted over the interval $x=-3$ to $x=3$. Estimate the area between the parabola and the $x$-axis by finding the area of four trapezia and two triangles that approximate this region, as shown.

Note: First find the height of each of the vertical lines drawn below.

spec.description: Equation-driven parabola and straight sampled joins at every integer from -3 to 3. Four trapezia and two triangles remain distinct through internal vertical boundaries and alternating light blue fill. The source has no y-scale, grid, axis arrows or axis titles.
spec.mathematics: y=x^2/4 on [-3,3]; sampled heights 9/4,1,1/4,0,1/4,1,9/4. These derived heights are used geometrically without printing answer labels.
spec.answerVisibility: Only source x-axis labels are visible; sampled heights and areas are withheld.

answer.short:
$\dfrac{19}{4}$ square units.

Add the four unit-width trapezia and two triangles using heights from $y=\frac14x^2$.
answer.worked:
The heights at $x=-3,-2,-1,0,1,2,3$ are $\frac94,1,\frac14,0,\frac14,1,\frac94$, respectively. Each strip has width $1$. By symmetry, calculate the three strips on one side and double.

$$\begin{align*} A_{\text{triangle}}&=\frac12(1)\left(\frac14\right)=\frac18,\\ A_{\text{inner trapezium}}&=\frac12(1)\left(\frac14+1\right)=\frac58,\\ A_{\text{outer trapezium}}&=\frac12(1)\left(1+\frac94\right)=\frac{13}{8},\\ A_{\text{estimate}}&=2\left(\frac18+\frac58+\frac{13}{8}\right),\\ A_{\text{estimate}}&=\frac{19}{4}\text{ square units}. \end{align*}$$

content.prompt: Two squares, one of side length 1, the other of side length 2, stand side by side. A straight line through the vertex of the smaller square cuts the area of the larger square in the ratio $2:1$. In what ratio does this line cut the area of the smaller square?

spec.description: Adjacent squares with aligned bases; smaller square on the left. A line runs from its bottom-left vertex through the common boundary to the larger square's right edge.
spec.mathematics: Square side lengths are 1 and 2. The line is straight; no additional heights are supplied.
spec.answerVisibility: Question contains only the supplied lengths and dividing line.

answer.short:
$5:1$.

Use the trapezium in the larger square to find the line's height at the common boundary.
answer.worked:
Let $x$ be the height of the line at the common boundary. Since the horizontal distances from the starting vertex are 1 and 3, its height at the right edge is $3x$.

The lower region in the larger square is a trapezium:
$$\begin{align*}A_{\text{lower, large}}&=\frac{(x+3x)\times2}{2}\\A_{\text{lower, large}}&=4x.\end{align*}$$
The diagram shows the upper region is larger, so
$$\begin{align*}4-4x&=2(4x)\\4&=12x\\x&=\frac13.\end{align*}$$
In the smaller square,
$$\begin{align*}A_{\text{lower, small}}&=\frac{1\times\frac13}{2}\\A_{\text{lower, small}}&=\frac16,\\A_{\text{upper, small}}&=1-\frac16\\A_{\text{upper, small}}&=\frac56.\end{align*}$$
Thus the upper-to-lower area ratio is $\frac56:\frac16=5:1$.

content.prompt: Suppose a convex quadrilateral has diagonals of length $p$ and $q$ and that they are perpendicular.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Using a simple example, show that the quadrilateral may not be a kite.

answer.short: For example, join $(-1,0)$, $(0,1)$, $(3,0)$ and $(0,-2)$ in order. The diagonals are perpendicular, but all four side lengths differ.
answer.worked:
Join $(-1,0)$, $(0,1)$, $(3,0)$ and $(0,-2)$ in order. This is a convex quadrilateral. One diagonal is horizontal and the other vertical, so they are perpendicular.

Its side lengths, found using Pythagoras' theorem, are $\sqrt2$, $\sqrt{10}$, $\sqrt{13}$ and $\sqrt5$. They are all different, so there are no two pairs of equal adjacent sides. Hence it is not a kite.

spec.description: Authored simple counterexample with perpendicular diagonals and no equal side pairs.
spec.mathematics: Vertices (-1,0), (0,1), (3,0), (0,-2) in cyclic order; side lengths squared are 2, 10, 13 and 5.
spec.answerVisibility: Solution only.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Nonetheless, explain why the area of such a quadrilateral is still given by $A=\dfrac{pq}{2}$.

answer.short:
$A=\dfrac{pq}{2}$.

The quadrilateral occupies half its enclosing rectangle of side lengths $p$ and $q$.
answer.worked:
Take the diagonal of length $p$ as the common base of the two triangles making up the quadrilateral. Let their perpendicular heights be $u$ and $v$. The other diagonal is perpendicular to this base, so $u+v=q$.
$$\begin{align*}A&=\frac{pu}{2}+\frac{pv}{2}\\A&=\frac{p(u+v)}{2}\\A&=\frac{pq}{2}.\end{align*}$$
Equivalently, these triangles occupy half the enclosing rectangle of width $p$ and height $u+v=q$.

answer.short:
$A=\dfrac{pq}{2}$.

Pythagoras' theorem in the four right triangles gives $a^2+c^2=b^2+d^2$, so the squared difference in the supplied formula is zero.
answer.worked:
Let the diagonals meet at $O$. Label the vertices $B,C,D,E$ in order, with $BC=a$, $CD=b$, $DE=c$ and $EB=d$. Put $OB=x$, $OC=y$, $OD=z$ and $OE=w$. The perpendicular diagonals form four right triangles. By Pythagoras' theorem,
$$\begin{align*}a^2&=x^2+y^2\\b^2&=y^2+z^2\\c^2&=z^2+w^2\\d^2&=w^2+x^2.\end{align*}$$
Thus
$$\begin{align*}a^2+c^2&=x^2+y^2+z^2+w^2\\a^2+c^2&=b^2+d^2\\a^2+c^2-b^2-d^2&=0.\end{align*}$$
Substituting into the supplied formula,
$$\begin{align*}A&=\frac14\sqrt{4p^2q^2-0^2}\\A&=\frac14(2pq)\\A&=\frac{pq}{2}.\end{align*}$$
Here $p$ and $q$ are positive lengths.

answer.worked:

$$\begin{align*}\text{Shaded fraction}&=\frac{\pi R^2-2\pi(R/2)^2-2\pi(R/3)^2}{\pi R^2}\\\text{Shaded fraction}&=1-\frac12-\frac29\\\text{Shaded fraction}&=\frac5{18}.\end{align*}$$

children.prompt: A circle is inscribed in an equilateral triangle. Find the circle’s area as a fraction of the triangle’s area.

spec.description: Upright equilateral triangle, inscribed circle and three radii to its tangency points. No dimensions or labels are supplied.
spec.mathematics: Vertices (-sqrt(3),0), (sqrt(3),0), (0,3); centre (0,1), radius 1. Tangencies are (0,0) and (±sqrt(3)/2,3/2). Coordinates define proportions only.
spec.answerVisibility: Question figure contains only supplied geometry.

answer.short:
$\dfrac{\pi}{3\sqrt3}$.

Split the triangle into three triangles with height equal to the circle’s radius.
answer.worked:
Let the circle have radius $r$ and the triangle have side length $s$. The centre is also the triangle’s centroid, so the triangle’s altitude is $3r$. Half the triangle has perpendicular sides $s/2$ and $3r$, and hypotenuse $s$. By Pythagoras,
$$\begin{align*}s^2&=\left(\frac{s}{2}\right)^2+(3r)^2\\\frac{3s^2}{4}&=9r^2\\s^2&=12r^2\\s&=2\sqrt3\,r\end{align*}$$
The three triangles formed by joining the centre to the vertices each have base $s$ and height $r$.
$$\begin{align*}A_{\triangle}&=3\left(\frac12sr\right)\\A_{\triangle}&=3\sqrt3\,r^2\\\frac{A_{\text{circle}}}{A_{\triangle}}&=\frac{\pi r^2}{3\sqrt3\,r^2}\\\frac{A_{\text{circle}}}{A_{\triangle}}&=\frac{\pi}{3\sqrt3}\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: A circle circumscribes an equilateral triangle. Find the triangle’s area as a fraction of the circle’s area.

spec.description: Circle circumscribing an upright equilateral triangle, with three segments from the centre to its vertices.
spec.mathematics: Unit circumcircle centred at (0,0); vertices (0,1), (-sqrt(3)/2,-1/2), (sqrt(3)/2,-1/2). No numerical givens are printed.
spec.answerVisibility: Question figure contains only supplied geometry.

answer.short:
$\dfrac{3\sqrt3}{4\pi}$.

Use the triangle’s altitude $3R/2$, where $R$ is the circle’s radius.
answer.worked:
Let the circle have radius $R$ and the triangle have side length $s$. The centre is the centroid, so the altitude is $3R/2$ and the distance from the centre to the base is $R/2$. Pythagoras gives
$$\begin{align*}\left(\frac{s}{2}\right)^2&=R^2-\left(\frac R2\right)^2\\\left(\frac{s}{2}\right)^2&=\frac{3R^2}{4}\\s&=\sqrt3\,R\\A_{\triangle}&=\frac12\left(\sqrt3\,R\right)\left(\frac{3R}{2}\right)\\A_{\triangle}&=\frac{3\sqrt3}{4}R^2\\\frac{A_{\triangle}}{A_{\text{circle}}}&=\frac{\frac{3\sqrt3}{4}R^2}{\pi R^2}\\\frac{A_{\triangle}}{A_{\text{circle}}}&=\frac{3\sqrt3}{4\pi}\end{align*}$$

content.prompt: Two semicircles are drawn in a quarter circle, as shown in the diagram below. Show that the areas $A_1$ and $A_2$ indicated in the diagram are equal.

spec.description: Quarter circle with inward semicircles on its vertical and horizontal radii. All three arcs and labels A₁ and A₂ are retained. White identifies the uncovered region A₂; light blue identifies semicircles and solid blue their overlap.
spec.mathematics: Quarter circle centred at (0,0), radius 2. Semicircles have centres (0,1) and (1,0), radius 1, and intersect at (0,0) and (1,1).
spec.answerVisibility: Only the supplied regions and labels are shown; no answer measurements are added.

answer.short:
$A_1=A_2$.

The two semicircle areas together equal the quarter-circle area; their overlap balances the uncovered region.
answer.worked:
Let each semicircle have radius $r$. The quarter circle has radius $2r$.
$$\begin{align*}A_{\text{two semicircles}}&=2\left(\frac12\pi r^2\right)\\A_{\text{two semicircles}}&=\pi r^2\\A_{\text{quarter circle}}&=\frac14\pi(2r)^2\\A_{\text{quarter circle}}&=\pi r^2\end{align*}$$
Let $B$ be the area covered by exactly one semicircle. Adding the semicircle areas counts the overlap twice, whereas the quarter circle contains the overlap once and also contains $A_2$.
$$\begin{align*}B+2A_1&=B+A_1+A_2\\A_1&=A_2\end{align*}$$

content.prompt: Four quarter circles each of radius $r$ intersect as shown in the diagram below. Determine the areas $A_1$, $A_2$ and $A_3$ indicated in the diagram, in terms of $r$.

spec.description: Square with four complete corner-centred quarter-circle arcs. Unfilled side regions, light-purple intermediate regions and purple central region distinguish the three requested area types.
spec.mathematics: Square side r; all four circle radii r. Adjacent-circle intersections occur at offsets r/2 and sqrt(3)r/2. Four congruent A1 regions, four congruent A2 regions and one A3 region partition the square.
spec.answerVisibility: Only the supplied region labels are visible; no calculated areas or auxiliary construction labels are included.

answer.short:
$A_1=\left(1-\frac{\sqrt3}{4}-\frac{\pi}{6}\right)r^2$, $A_2=\left(\frac{\sqrt3}{2}-1+\frac{\pi}{12}\right)r^2$, $A_3=\left(1-\sqrt3+\frac{\pi}{3}\right)r^2$.

Use sectors and triangles for $A_1$, then symmetry and the total quarter-circle areas.
answer.worked:
The square has side $r$. The intersection of the two circles centred at the right-hand corners forms an equilateral triangle with those corners. Their overlap inside the square consists of two $60^\circ$ sectors less an equilateral triangle. Let its area be $L$.

$$\begin{align*}L&=2\left(\frac{60}{360}\pi r^2\right)-\frac12r\left(\frac{\sqrt3}{2}r\right)\\L&=\left(\frac{\pi}{3}-\frac{\sqrt3}{4}\right)r^2.\end{align*}$$

The left-hand region $A_1$ lies outside both right-centred quarter circles.

$$\begin{align*}A_1&=r^2-\left(2\cdot\frac14\pi r^2-L\right)\\A_1&=\left(1-\frac{\sqrt3}{4}-\frac{\pi}{6}\right)r^2.\end{align*}$$

By symmetry, the square contains four regions of area $A_1$, four of area $A_2$ and one of area $A_3$. These regions belong to two, three and four quarter circles respectively. Hence

$$\begin{align*}4A_1+4A_2+A_3&=r^2\\8A_1+12A_2+4A_3&=\pi r^2.\end{align*}$$

Subtract the second equation from four times the first:

$$\begin{align*}8A_1+4A_2&=(4-\pi)r^2\\A_2&=\left(1-\frac\pi4\right)r^2-2A_1\\A_2&=\left(\frac{\sqrt3}{2}-1+\frac{\pi}{12}\right)r^2.\end{align*}$$

Finally,

$$\begin{align*}A_3&=r^2-4A_1-4A_2\\A_3&=\left(1-\sqrt3+\frac\pi3\right)r^2.\end{align*}$$

and consider the cases
and

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}2ab+2ac+2bc&=52\\ab+ac+bc&=26\end{align*}$$
If $a\ge3$, then $b\ge4$ and $c\ge5$, so $ab+ac+bc\ge12+15+20=47$. Thus $a=1$ or $a=2$.

For $a=1$:
$$\begin{align*}b+c+bc&=26\\(b+1)(c+1)&=27\end{align*}$$
The factor pair satisfying $1<b<c$ is $3\times9$, giving $b=2$ and $c=8$.

For $a=2$:
$$\begin{align*}2b+2c+bc&=26\\(b+2)(c+2)&=30\end{align*}$$
The factor pair satisfying $2<b<c$ is $5\times6$, giving $b=3$ and $c=4$.

Therefore $(a,b,c)=(1,2,8)$ or $(2,3,4)$.

content.prompt: An ant walks from $A$ to $B$ along the upper surface of the square-based pyramid shown below. What is the length of the shortest such path? Hint: flatten the pyramid.

spec.description: Right square-based pyramid on an outlined plane. A and B are opposite base vertices; the front base edge is 3 cm and a lateral edge is 4 cm. The base diagonal is dashed. Decorative blue fills are omitted and hidden edges use dashed strokes.
spec.mathematics: Square base side 3 cm; equal lateral edges 4 cm; A and B opposite. The dashed base diagonal is not an upper-surface route.
spec.answerVisibility: No shortest path drawn on the question figure.

inlines.text: Unfold two adjacent faces; the shortest route is a straight line across their net.

answer.worked:
Unfold two adjacent triangular faces. Their outer sides are $4,4,3,3\text{ cm}$ and their shared edge is $4\text{ cm}$. The shortest route is the straight segment $AB$ in this net.

Let half the route be $x\text{ cm}$ and let the upper part of the shared edge be $h\text{ cm}$.
$$\begin{align*}x^2+h^2&=16\\x^2+(4-h)^2&=9\\h^2-(4-h)^2&=7\\8h-16&=7\\h&=\frac{23}{8}\\x^2&=16-\left(\frac{23}{8}\right)^2\\x^2&=\frac{495}{64}\\x&=\frac{3\sqrt{55}}8\end{align*}$$
The shortest path is $2x=\dfrac{3\sqrt{55}}4\text{ cm}$.

spec.description: Two adjacent triangular faces unfolded about their shared 4 cm edge. The straight route joins A to B and is divided into two equal lengths x by the perpendicular shared edge.
spec.mathematics: Outer sides 4,4,3,3 cm; shared edge h + (4-h) = 4 cm; x²+h² = 16 and x²+(4-h)² = 9.

answer.worked:
$$xyz=36.$$

answer.short: Fill one tank. Tilt the empty tank with a corner lowest, and transfer water into it until the surface passes through the three vertices adjacent to that corner. This transfers $\frac16\times120=20$ litres, leaving 100 litres in the first tank.
answer.worked:
Fill tank A completely. Hold empty tank B with one bottom corner lowest. Tilt it so the three vertices joined by edges to that corner lie in a horizontal plane. Pour water from A into B until the surface reaches those three vertices.

The water in B forms a triangular-based pyramid. If the tank dimensions are $l$, $w$ and $h$, its triangular base has area $\frac12lw$ and its perpendicular height is $h$.
$$\begin{align*}V_{\text{water in B}}&=\frac13\left(\frac12lw\right)h\\V_{\text{water in B}}&=\frac16lwh\\V_{\text{water in B}}&=\frac16(120)\\V_{\text{water in B}}&=20\text{ L}.\end{align*}$$
Tank A therefore contains $120-20=100$ litres.

answer.short:

A spherical octant has one-eighth of the sphere's curved surface and three quarter-circle faces.
answer.worked:
The sketch is a spherical octant with three perpendicular quarter-circle faces.
$$\begin{align*}V&=\frac{1}{8}\times\frac{4}{3}\pi r^3\\V&=\frac{1}{8}\times\frac{4}{3}\pi(2)^3\\V&=\frac{4\pi}{3}\text{ cm}^3\end{align*}$$
Add one-eighth of the sphere's curved area and the three exposed quarter-circle faces.
$$\begin{align*}A&=\frac{1}{8}(4\pi r^2)+3\left(\frac{1}{4}\pi r^2\right)\\A&=\frac{1}{8}(4\pi(2)^2)+3\left(\frac{1}{4}\pi(2)^2\right)\\A&=5\pi\text{ cm}^2\end{align*}$$

children.prompt: Find the volume of the sphere.

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}4\pi r^2&=1\\r^2&=\frac{1}{4\pi}\\r&=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{\pi}}\\V_{\text{sphere}}&=\frac43\pi\left(\frac{1}{2\sqrt{\pi}}\right)^3\\V_{\text{sphere}}&=\frac{1}{6\sqrt{\pi}}\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Find the volume of the cube.

answer.worked:
Let the cube's edge length be $s$.
$$\begin{align*}6s^2&=1\\s&=\frac{1}{\sqrt6}\\V_{\text{cube}}&=\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt6}\right)^3\\V_{\text{cube}}&=\frac{1}{6\sqrt6}\end{align*}$$

children.prompt: Which has the greater volume, the sphere or the cube? Answer this without using your calculator.

answer.worked:
Since $\pi<4<6$, we have $\sqrt\pi<\sqrt6$. Therefore,
$$\frac{1}{6\sqrt\pi}>\frac{1}{6\sqrt6}.$$
The sphere has the greater volume.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Find the surface area of the cube.

answer.worked:
Let the cube's edge length be $s$.
$$\begin{align*}s^3&=1\\s&=1\\A_{\text{cube}}&=6(1)^2\\A_{\text{cube}}&=6\end{align*}$$

children.label: c
children.prompt: Which has the smaller surface area, the sphere or the cube? Answer this without using your calculator.

answer.worked:
Since $\pi<4<6$, we have $36\pi<216$. Therefore,
$$\sqrt[3]{36\pi}<\sqrt[3]{216}=6.$$
The sphere has the smaller surface area.

entries.description: 12A Perimeter
entries.exclusionReason: Standalone teaching heading; retain as source topic identity, not a practice block.

entries.description: The word perimeter can either refer to the boundary of a planar region, or to the length of that boundary. We will mainly be concerned with regions that have straight sides; however, we later consider regions bounded by circular arcs.
entries.exclusionReason: Standalone definition and teaching introduction.

entries.description: Squares. The perimeter of a square of dimensions x × x is P = 4x.
entries.exclusionReason: Standalone formula teaching.

entries.description: Square with x beside the left side and x beneath the bottom side; cyan interior and dark boundary.

presentation.mathematicalMeaning: Both adjacent side lengths are x.

entries.exclusionReason: Meaningful mathematical diagram belonging to excluded standalone teaching.

entries.description: Rectangles. The perimeter of a rectangle of dimensions x × y is P = 2x + 2y.
entries.exclusionReason: Standalone formula teaching.

entries.description: Horizontal rectangle with y beside the left side and x beneath the bottom side; cyan interior and dark boundary.

presentation.mathematicalMeaning: Horizontal side x and vertical side y.

entries.exclusionReason: Meaningful mathematical diagram belonging to excluded standalone teaching.

entries.description: Two worked rectangle-dimension examples, arranged side by side, with their solutions beneath the corresponding prompts.
entries.exclusionReason: Standalone worked example; reference evidence only under practice-only scope.

entries.description: The ratio of length to width of a rectangle is 3 : 5. Find its dimensions if its perimeter is 80 cm.
entries.exclusionReason: Part of excluded standalone Example 1.

entries.description: The width of a rectangle is 2 cm longer than its length. Find its dimensions if its perimeter is 24 cm.
entries.exclusionReason: Part of excluded standalone Example 1.

entries.description: Solution
entries.exclusionReason: Heading for supplied worked-example solutions.

entries.description:
Let 3x cm and 5x cm be the length and width of the rectangle, respectively. Then
2(3x) + 2(5x) = 80
16x = 80
x = 5.
The rectangle has dimensions 15 cm × 25 cm.

presentation.method: Represent the ratio dimensions with a common multiplier and solve the perimeter equation.
presentation.workingAlignment: Successive equations aligned at their equals signs.

entries.exclusionReason: Supplied solution to excluded standalone Example 1(a); transcribed without independent solving.

entries.description: Horizontal rectangle with 3x cm beside the left side and 5x cm beneath the bottom side; pink interior and dark boundary.
entries.exclusionReason: Meaningful mathematical diagram accompanying an excluded worked-example solution.

entries.description:
Let x cm and (x + 2) cm be the length and width of the rectangle, respectively. Then
2x + 2(x + 2) = 24
4x + 4 = 24
x = 5.
The rectangle has dimensions 5 cm × 7 cm.

presentation.method: Represent dimensions as x and x + 2 and solve the perimeter equation.
presentation.workingAlignment: Successive equations aligned at their equals signs.

entries.exclusionReason: Supplied solution to excluded standalone Example 1(b); transcribed without independent solving.

entries.description: The red line segments have total length 2 × 12. The blue line segments have total length 2 × 20. Therefore, the perimeter is P = 2 × 12 + 2 × 20 = 64.

entries.description: Luna measures three sides of a rectangle, and their lengths total to 27 cm. Mateo measures three sides of the same rectangle, and their lengths total to 33 cm. Find the perimeter of the rectangle.

entries.description:
Informal argument. Consider any circle. If we take an exact copy of this circle and enlarge it, every part of the new circle is simply a scaled version of the original.
• The new circle is still a perfect circle.
• The diameter grows by the same factor as the circumference.
• Because both increase proportionally, their ratio remains unchanged.

entries.description: This means that no matter how big or small a circle is, the relationship between its circumference and diameter must always be the same. Since this holds for all circles, the ratio is a universal constant, which we call π, which we (incorrectly) pronounce as “pie”.

entries.description:
Defining π. Take any circle of circumference C, diameter d and radius r. We define π to be the ratio of C to d:

entries.description:
Babylonians calculated the area of a circle by taking three times the square of its radius, implying that π = 3. One Babylonian tablet suggests a more accurate value of 3⅛. The first recorded algorithm for approximating the value of π was a geometrical approach using polygons, devised around 250 BC by the Greek mathematician Archimedes, who proved that 223/71 < π < 22/7. You will encounter this idea in a subsequent exercise, where you will prove a less impressive result: 3 < π < 4. Of course, better approximations are known. In fact, the first nine decimal digits of π are 3.14159265, and these can be recalled from the mnemonic:
HOW I WISH I COULD CALCULATE PI EASILY TODAY
The number of letters in each word is equal to the corresponding digit of π. This gives many more digits than the standard approximation: π = 3.14. In the 1760s Johann Heinrich Lambert proved that π is irrational: that is, it cannot be expressed as the ratio of two integers.
entries.exclusionReason: Standalone historical teaching and mnemonic; reference evidence only.

entries.description: Think of the circle as a series of concentric circular ropes. Cutting and then unwrapping these into straight lines will form a figure resembling a triangle with height r. Its base is the circumference of a circle, 2πr. If we took thinner and thinner ropes, then the area of the figure would approach the area of a triangle. Finding the area of this triangle will give the area of the circle: A = ½ · base · height = ½ · 2πr · r = πr².

entries.description: Cut the circle into identical slices. Arrange these into the figure resembling a parallelogram shown below the circle. If we cut successively more slices, then the length of the base would approach half of the circle circumference, and the height would approach the circle radius. In the limit, the figure becomes a rectangle of width ½ · (2πr) and height r. Therefore, A = base · height = ½ · (2πr) · r = πr².

entries.description:
Prisms
One way to build a three-dimensional figure is to construct it from polygons. Recall that the name for such a figure is a polyhedron. A common example is a prism, which is a polyhedron with two identical parallel faces (called the base and top), with all its other faces being parallelograms. When these other faces are all perpendicular to the base we call the prism a right prism. If a right prism is stood on its base, then these other faces are vertical rectangles. In what follows when we use the terminology “prism” we implicitly mean a right prism. Prisms are named based on their polygon base, for example a triangular prism has a triangle as base. A prism has uniform cross-section, which means that every slice through the figure is identical to the base. The cross-sections of the prisms below appear as orange slices. The area of each slice is always the same.

entries.description: A circular cone is a surface that tapers smoothly from a circular base to a point called the apex. The apex of a right circular cone lies directly above the centre of the circular base. We will usually simply call such a surface a cone. In this section we establish the formula for the surface area of a right circular cone.

entries.description: Consider a cone of radius r and slant length s. Cutting and then laying the cone flat will give the blue sector on the right. The circumference of the original cone is equal to the arc length of the sector. The area of the sector can be found by comparing the length of the red arc with the length of the green circumference. We find that A = (red length / green length) × whole area = (2πr / 2πs) × πs² = πrs.

entries.description:
To deduce the above formula, we first consider the volume of a pyramid whose base has dimensions a × a and whose height is a/2. Six copies of this pyramid fit exactly into a cube of dimensions a × a × a. The volume of this pyramid is therefore ⅙a³.
We then stretch this pyramid in the horizontal direction by a factor of b/a so that the new base has dimensions a × b. We also stretch the pyramid in the vertical direction by a factor of 2h/a so that its new height is h. The volume will also scale by each of these scale factors so that the final volume is
V = ⅙a³ × (2h/a) × (b/a) = ⅓abh.

entries.description:
To find the area of the base we first use the Pythagorean Theorem to find the value of x indicated in the diagram:
x = √(7² − 6²) = √13.
Recall that the area A cm² of the square base is half the product of its diagonals. Therefore,
A = (2x)²/2 = (2√13)²/2 = 26.
Therefore,
V = ⅓Ah = ⅓(26)(6) = 52.
The volume of the pyramid is 52 cm³.

entries.description:
Every horizontal slice of this figure will give a circle inscribed in a square. To find the fraction of each square slice taken up by the circle we consider the base of the pyramid. The area of the circle is A = πr². The area of the square is A = (2r)² = 4r². The fraction of the square taken up by the circle is then
A(circle)/A(square) = πr²/(4r²) = π/4.

entries.description:
To find the area of a prism we multiply the area of its base by its height. We have sliced the right triangular prism below into seven identical sections each parallel to its base. Each section has then been slid to the right to form a slanted solid. Notice the jagged edges of the slanted solid.

Since the right triangular prism and the slanted solid are composed of the same cut up sections, they have the same volume. We increase the number of slices so the thickness of the sections becomes extremely small. The slanted solid we obtain in the limit is called an oblique prism. The right triangular prism and the oblique triangular prism will have the same volume.

entries.description:
Applying Cavalieri’s principle, the volume inside the hemisphere equals the volume outside of the cone. Thus,
V(hemisphere) = V(cylinder) − V(cone)
= πr³ − (1/3)πr³
= (2/3)πr³
⇒ V(sphere) = (4/3)πr³.

entries.description:
Therefore,
V(sphere) = sum of volumes of the pyramids
= (1/3)Br + ⋯ + (1/3)Br
= (1/3)r(B + ⋯ + B)
= (1/3)r · A(sphere)
⇒ (4/3)πr³ = (1/3)r · A(sphere)
A(sphere) = 4πr².

entries.description:
We first find the radius r of the sphere:
V = 4πr³/3
36π = 4πr³/3
27 = r³
r = 3.
Therefore, the surface area is A = 4πr² = 4π(3²) = 36π cm².
